أبيض.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine بَيْضَاء bayḍāʾ > Levantine بيضا) from root ب-ي-ض (b-y-ḍ, 'whiteness, brightness; egg').

أخ.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *'aḫ- ('brother'), one of the core biradical kinship nouns across Semitic languages.
أخ.notes: Before possessive suffixes or in construct, the long stem vowel resurfaces (أخوي 'my brother', أخوك 'your brother'), and the dual is أخوين ('two brothers').

أخضر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine خَضْرَاء > Levantine خضرا) from Semitic root خ-ض-ر (ḫ-ḍ-r, 'fresh green growth, herbs, vegetables').

أزرق.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine زَرْقَاء > Levantine زرقا) from root ز-ر-ق (z-r-q, 'clear blue, gleaming sky/water').

أسود.etymology: Formed on the colour/defect elative pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine فَعْلَاء sawdāʾ > Levantine سودا) from root س-و-د (s-w-d, 'black, dark').

أصفر.etymology: Primary colour adjective on the pattern أَفْعَل (afʿal, feminine صَفْرَاء > Levantine صفرا) from root ص-ف-ر (ṣ-f-r, 'yellow, golden-pale, gleaming brass').

أصيل.etymology: Adjective أَصِيل ('genuine, authentic, deep-rooted') on the pattern فَعِيل from أَصْل ('root, origin, foundation', root ء-ص-ل): literally 'firmly rooted in its true nature'.

أغنية.etymology: Derived on the pattern أُفْعولة (ufʿūla) from the root غ-ن-ي (gh-n-y), whose Form II verb غَنَّى (ghannā) means 'to sing, chant melodiously'.

أنف.etymology: Ancient Proto-Semitic body-part noun أَنْف ('nose; proud promontory') from `*ʾanp-`, preserving the original medial `-n-` that assimilated to `-pp-` in Northwest Semitic.

إبريق.etymology: Early borrowing into Classical Arabic from Middle Persian *ābrēz / ābrēg* ('water-pourer', from *āb* 'water' + *rēxtan* 'to pour').
إبريق.notes: Names a spouted teapot, kettle, or pitcher (plural أباريق).

إسفنجة.etymology: Singulative noun إِسْفَنْجَة ('a sponge') from collective إِسْفَنْج, borrowed in antiquity from Greek σπόγγος / σφόγγος ('sea sponge')—the same Mediterranean source behind English 'sponge'.

cognates.meaning: cleaning sponge, from the same Greek source

إيقاع.etymology: Form IV verbal noun إِيقَاع ('rhythm, cadence') from the root و-ق-ع ('fall, land in beats'): literally 'letting beats fall in measured time', established since al-Kindi and al-Farabi as the core Arabic term for musical rhythm.

احتاج.etymology: Form VIII verb (افتعل) from the root ح-و-ج (h-w-j), associated with need, want, and necessity.
احتاج.notes: In everyday Jordanian conversation, speakers often use the active participle محتاج ('needing, in need of') alongside بده.

اسم.etymology: An ancient Proto-Semitic basic noun (*šim- 'name'), written in Arabic with an initial prosthetic vowel (همزة الوصل) before the two root consonants س-م.
اسم.notes: Cognates appear across every branch of Semitic, making اسم one of the oldest everyday words in Arabic.

الأحد.etymology: Short for يَوْم الأَحَد ('day one / the first day'), built from the Semitic numeral root ء-ح-د ('one') on the stem أَحَد. Alongside الإثنين ('Monday, day two'), الثلاثاء ('Tuesday, day three'), الأربعاء ('Wednesday, day four'), and الخميس ('Thursday, day five'), it preserves the ancient Near Eastern numbered-day week.

الأربعا.etymology: Spoken Levantine form of يَوْم الْأَرْبِعَاء (yawm al-ʾarbiʿāʾ, 'the fourth day'), derived from the Semitic numeral root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ, 'four').

الخميس.etymology: Short for يَوْم الْخَمِيس (yawm al-ḫamīs, 'the fifth day'), built on pattern فَعِيل from the Semitic numeral root خ-م-س (ḫ-m-s, 'five').

السبت.etymology: From Classical Arabic السَّبْت (as-sabt, 'Saturday, Sabbath'), from Semitic root س-ب-ت (s-b-t, 'to rest, cease work at week's end'), cognate with Hebrew Šabbāṯ and Aramaic Šabbəṯā.

باب.etymology: An ancient Semitic word for 'door, gate, entrance' (already attested in Akkadian *bābu* and Aramaic *bābā*).
باب.notes: Yields the derived feminine noun بوابة ('outer gate, portal') for the iron courtyard entrance.

بابونج.etymology: Classical Arabic botanical and medical term بَابُونَج ('chamomile'), borrowed during the Abbasid pharmacological era from Middle Persian bābūnag (modern Persian بابونه bābūneh) and treasured across Levantine households as a calming evening tea.

بحر.etymology: Classical Arabic noun بَحْر ('sea, great river', plural بِحَار / بُحُور) from the Semitic root ب-ح-ر ('wide cleft expanse of water'), used metaphorically in classical poetry for boundless generosity and for poetic meters.

بداية.etymology: Noun بِدَايَة ('beginning, opening') from the root ب-د-ء / ب-د-ي ('begin, start first'), paired naturally with نِهَايَة ('ending').

برق.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic noun بَرْق ('lightning') from the root ب-ر-ق ('flash, gleam, shine brightly').

بندورة.etymology: Levantine borrowing بَنْدُورَة ('tomato') from Italian pomodoro (literally pomo d'oro, 'golden apple'), adapted into Eastern Mediterranean Arabic when New World tomatoes arrived via Italian port trade in the 18th–19th centuries.

بوابة.etymology: Augmented feminine noun بَوَّابَة ('main gate, arched portal', plural بَوَّابَات) derived on the intensive pattern فَعَّالَة from بَاب ('door', root ب-و-ب), naming a grand courtyard or street entrance larger than an ordinary room door.

بيت.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *bayt- ('house, dwelling'), related to the verbal root ب-ي-ت ('to spend the night').
بيت.notes: The same Semitic word gave rise to the Phoenician letter name *bēt* ('house'), ancestor of Greek beta (Β). In Amman, بيت names both a family home and a traditional courtyard house.

تاريخ.etymology: Verbal noun (تَفْعِيل) of Form II أَرَّخَ (ʾarraḫa, 'to date a letter or chronicle'), linked to the Semitic moon/month word *warḫ- (compare Hebrew yārēaḥ 'moon', yereḥ 'month'): fixing an event by month and day.

تذكرة.etymology: Verbal noun of Form II ذَكَّرَ ('to remind'), built on the root ذ-ك-ر ('remember, mention') with the pattern تَفْعِلَة: originally 'a written reminder or memorandum', whence Ottoman and modern Arabic specialized it to a travel or admission 'ticket'.

تراث.etymology: Classical Arabic تُرَاث (turāṯ, 'heritage, inheritance'), formed with regular initial w -> t assimilation (*wurāṯ > turāṯ) from root و-ر-ث (w-r-ṯ, 'to inherit').

تلة.etymology: Singulative noun تَلَّة ('a hill') from collective تَلّ ('mound, hillock'), rooted in ت-ل-ل and shared across ancient Mesopotamian and Levantine topography (familiar in archaeology as 'tell', a layered settlement mound).

cognates.meaning: Middle Eastern archaeological mound, borrowed from Arabic تَلّ

تلج.etymology: Levantine pronunciation تَلْج (talj, 'ice; snow') of Classical Arabic ثَلْج (ṯalj), inherited from Proto-Semitic `*ṯalg-` ('snow,winter ice') with regular urban Levantine shift of interdental ث (ṯ) to ت (t).

جبل.etymology: Inherited Semitic noun جَبَل ('mountain') from the triliteral root ج-ب-ل ('to form, mould, rise as a massif'). In Amman, جبل also designates the city's historic neighbourhoods perched across rolling limestone hills (such as Jabal Amman and Jabal al-Weibdeh).

جبين.etymology: Inherited Semitic body-part noun جَبِين ('forehead, brow') on the pattern فَعِيل from the root ج-ب-ن, originally denoting the prominent upper brow ridge on either side of the forehead.

جريدة.etymology: Originally Classical Arabic جَرِيدَة (jarīda, 'stripped palm-branch stalk' used as a writing tally or dispatch roll), from root ج-ر-د ('to strip leaves/bark'); adopted in the 19th century for 'newspaper'.

جزر.etymology: Collective noun جَزَر ('carrots', singulative جَزَرَة), borrowed in early Islamic agricultural trade from Middle Persian gazar (modern Persian گزر gazar) when purple, yellow, and orange root carrots spread westward from the Iranian plateau across the Levant.

جمعة.etymology: From the root ج-م-ع (j-m-', 'to gather, bring together'), naming Friday (يوم الجمعة) as the day of congregational gathering.
جمعة.notes: Unlike the earlier days of the week counted numerically from Sunday through Thursday, Friday takes its name from community assembly.

جنينة.etymology: Diminutive of جَنَّة (janna, 'garden, orchard'), from the triliteral root ج-ن-ن (j-n-n) expressing covering and dense foliage shading the ground. Standard Levantine word for a courtyard or home garden.

جوز.etymology: Classical Arabic collective noun جَوْز ('walnuts; walnut timber'), borrowed early from Middle Persian gōz ('walnut') and prized across Damascus and Amman for fine inlaid furniture and piano cabinetry (خشب جوز).

cognates.meaning: walnut, from the same Iranian source

حبر.etymology: Classical Arabic حِبْر (ḥibr, 'ink; beauty, fine mark'), from Semitic root ح-ب-ر (ḥ-b-r, 'to adorn, stripe, write finely with ink').

حديد.etymology: From the geminate root ح-د-د (h-d-d, 'to be sharp, keen, bounded'), originally describing sharpened metal and generalized in Arabic to 'iron'.
حديد.notes: Used for gates (بوابة حديد), heavy wrenches (مفتاح حديد), and hardware.

حذاء.etymology: Classical Arabic حِذَاء ('shoe, footwear', plural أَحْذِيَة) from the root ح-ذ-و ('place sole-to-sole, cut leather to match the foot's outline'), originally naming a strapped leather sandal cut to the exact measure of its wearer.

حليب.etymology: From the Proto-Semitic dairy root ح-ل-ب (*ḥ-l-b, 'to milk'), formed on the pattern فَعيل ('freshly milked milk').
حليب.notes: Whereas Classical لبن meant fresh milk, in Levantine Arabic حليب means fresh milk while لبن denotes yoghurt.

خبز.etymology: From the triliteral root خ-ب-ز (kh-b-z, 'to bake bread'), common across Arabic and Ethiopian Semitic.
خبز.notes: Fresh morning خبز is a staple of every Jordanian breakfast table.

خريف.etymology: Derived on pattern فَعِيل from root خ-ر-ف (ḫ-r-f, 'to pluck ripe fruit from trees'): originally the autumn fruit-picking and harvest season.

خشب.etymology: Native Arabic collective noun from خ-ش-ب (kh-sh-b), denoting timber and woodwork.
خشب.notes: Used directly in apposition after another noun in Jordanian Arabic to indicate material: درج خشب ('wooden stairs'), قطار خشب ('wooden train').

خل.etymology: Collective noun خَلّ ('vinegar') from the geminate Semitic root خ-ل-ل ('turn sour, ferment acidly'), naming wine or cider soured into household vinegar.

درج.etymology: From the root د-ر-ج (d-r-j, 'to step, advance gradually'), used collectively for a flight of stairs—or with different vowels (دُرج) for a desk drawer.
درج.notes: Amman's hillsides are famous for public stone staircases (أدراج) linking upper and lower streets.

دفتر.etymology: Borrowed via Persian *daftar* from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra, 'prepared hide, parchment, ledger').
دفتر.notes: Entered Classical Arabic early for an account register or ledger—just like Tariq's paper reception book.

راتب.etymology: From the triliteral root ر-ت-ب (r-t-b), expressing steadiness, order, and fixed arrangement. As an active participle راتب describes something regular and enduring, whence a fixed periodic salary.
راتب.notes: Used across modern Arabic for a regular monthly wage alongside مرتب.

ربيع.etymology: From the root ر-ب-ع (r-b-ʿ), connected with resting in lush pasture and spring rains that revive grazing land; hence the spring season across Arabic dialects.

رسالة.etymology: Derived on pattern فِعَالَة from root ر-س-ل (r-s-l, 'to send forth a messenger or dispatch'): anything sent, from a handwritten letter to a recorded voice message.

رصاص.etymology: Classical Arabic material noun رَصَاص (raṣāṣ / ruṣāṣ, 'lead, tin'), associated with root ر-ص-ص ('to press tightly together, solder with lead'); paired with قلم in قلم رصاص ('lead pencil').

رطوبة.etymology: Abstract quality noun رُطُوبَة ('dampness, moisture, humidity') formed on the pattern فُعُولَة from the root ر-ط-ب ('be moist, fresh, tender').

زيت.etymology: Primary noun زَيْت ('oil, originally olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean-Semitic Wanderwort tied to زَيْتُون ('olive tree/fruit'). Passed from Arabic into Iberian Romance as Spanish aceite and Portuguese azeite.

history.meaning: olive oil; cooking or lubricating oil

زيتون.etymology: Collective noun زَيْتُون ('olives; olive trees'), formed on زَيْت with the Semitic suffix ـُون. Borrowed directly from Arabic (الزَّيْتُونَة) into Spanish aceituna and Portuguese azeitona.

ساحة.etymology: From the hollow root س-و-ح (s-w-h, 'to spread out openly'), naming an open inner courtyard or public town square.
ساحة.notes: Traditional Amman houses organize rooms around a sheltered stone ساحة planted with trees and jasmine.

ساعاتي.etymology: Traditional Eastern Mediterranean craft noun سَاعَاتِيّ ('watchmaker, clockmaker'), formed by attaching the Ottoman Turkish occupational suffix -ci (adapted into Levantine Arabic after plural ساعات as ـاتي) to سَاعَة ('clock, watch').

ساعة.etymology: Classical Arabic noun meaning 'a short span of time, moment, hour', later extended to timepieces—both a wall clock (ساعة حيط) and a wristwatch.
ساعة.notes: Used in telling clock time across all varieties of Arabic.

سطل.etymology: Early Mediterranean loanword سَطْل ('bucket, pail', plural سُطُول), borrowed via Aramaic/Byzantine Greek σίτλα from Latin situla ('water bucket'). Still the everyday word for a bucket across Jordan, Palestine, Syria, and Lebanon.

سكر.etymology: Borrowed via Middle Persian *šakar* from Sanskrit *śárkarā* ('gravel, grit, crystallized sugar').
سكر.notes: Medieval Arabic trade carried السكر into European languages, producing Spanish *azúcar*, French *sucre*, and English 'sugar'.

سلة.etymology: Derived from the Semitic root س-ل-ل (s-l-l, 'to pull out, weave reeds'), originally naming a woven reed or wicker market basket.

سلم.etymology: Noun سُلَّم ('ladder, flight of steps; musical scale') from the root س-ل-م ('be safe, ascend safely step by step'), naming the runged wooden ladder because it carries a climber safely upward.

سهل.etymology: Adjective سَهْل ('easy, smooth, level') from the root س-ه-ل, which originally described soft, level lowland plains (سَهْل 'plain') free of rugged stones, and by natural metaphor came to mean 'easy, effortless'.

history.meaning: smooth plain; easy (also in أهلا وسهلا 'you have come to level, easy ground')

سوق.etymology: Ancient Semitic trade word (attested in Aramaic *šūqā*, 'street, marketplace'), naming an open-air or covered market.
سوق.notes: Frequently feminine in Arabic usage; plural أسواق.

شاحنة.etymology: Feminine active participle شَاحِنَة ('freight truck, lorry') from the root ش-ح-ن ('load cargo, fill a vessel'), coined in modern Arabic from سَيَّارَة شَاحِنَة ('cargo-carrying vehicle').

history.meaning: to load a ship with cargo

شارع.etymology: Active participle of ش-ر-ع (sh-r-', 'to open onto, lead into, set forth a path'), originally 'an open thoroughfare' and today 'street'.
شارع.notes: Takes the quadriliteral broken plural شوارع.

morphemes.meaning: opening a way, setting a path

شاي.etymology: Ultimately from Sinitic 茶 (chá, 'tea'), reaching Arabic along overland Silk Road trade routes via Persian چای (čây) and Ottoman Turkish çay.
شاي.notes: Languages supplied overland via Central Asia and Persia adopted 'cha/shay' forms, whereas maritime European trade from Fujian adopted 'tea/thé'.

شباك.etymology: From the root ش-ب-ك (sh-b-k, 'to interlace, entwine like a net'), originally naming the latticework grille or mashrabiya fitted across a window opening, and in Levantine Arabic the everyday word for 'window'.
شباك.notes: Compare Standard Arabic نافذة ('opening'); spoken Jordanian uses شباك (plural شبابيك) for windows and wooden shutters alike.

شمس.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *šamš- ('sun'), grammatically feminine in Arabic and famously the model word for 'sun letters' (الحروف الشمسية), since الشَّمْس assimilates the l of ال- into ash-shams.
شمس.notes: Contrasts with القمر ('the moon'), model for non-assimilating moon letters.

شنتة.etymology: Borrowed into Levantine and Egyptian Arabic from Ottoman Turkish *çanta* ('bag, pouch, suitcase').
شنتة.notes: In Amman شنتة (plural شناتي) covers handbags, backpacks, and travel suitcases.

شهري.etymology: Formed from شهر ('month') plus the relational nisba suffix ـي (-iyy), yielding 'monthly'.
شهري.notes: شهر itself is an inherited Semitic time noun originally tied to the new moon.

صابون.etymology: Early Mediterranean Wanderwort entering Arabic via Aramaic *ṣābūnā* from Late Latin *sāpō* ('soap'), then carried by Levantine olive-oil soapmakers back across medieval trade networks.
صابون.notes: Levantine olive-oil soap (from Nablus, Aleppo, and Salt) has been famous for over a millennium.

صحن.etymology: From Classical Arabic صَحْن (ṣaḥn, 'broad shallow dish, plate, open courtyard'), from root ص-ح-ن denoting a flat, open basin or saucer.

صخر.etymology: Collective noun صَخْر ('solid rock, boulders', singulative صَخْرَة) from the Semitic root ص-خ-ر, evoking immovable mountain bedrock—hence the proverbial simile ثابت متل الصخر ('steady as rock').

صفحة.etymology: Instance/surface noun from root ص-ف-ح (ṣ-f-ḥ, 'to flatten out, broaden a surface'): originally the flat side of a blade, cheek, or leaf of parchment, hence 'page'.

history.meaning: flat side; face of a sheet; page

صورة.etymology: From the root ص-و-ر (ṣ-w-r), expressing shaping, forming, and depicting; extended from 'form, image, likeness' to modern drawings and photographs.

صينية.etymology: Substantivized feminine nisba صِينِيَّة ('serving tray, round baking pan', plural صَوَانِي) from الصِّين ('China'): originally naming fine imported Chinese porcelain platters, and later extended across the Levant to brass, copper, and oven trays.

morphemes.meaning: Chinese platter -> serving or baking tray

طاولة.etymology: Levantine Arabic borrowing via Ottoman Turkish *tavla* or Mediterranean Romance *tavola* (from Latin *tabula*, 'board, plank, table').
طاولة.notes: Everyday word for a dining or café table across Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine.

طين.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *ṭīn- ('wet earth, potter's clay, mud'), preserved unchanged across Aramaic and Classical Arabic طِين (ṭīn).

عاصفة.etymology: Feminine active participle عَاصِفَة ('storm, gale', plural عَوَاصِف) from the root ع-ص-ف ('blow fiercely, sweep away chaff'), substantivized from رِيح عَاصِفَة ('tempestuous wind').

عدس.etymology: Inherited Semitic collective noun عَدَس ('lentils'), cultivated across the Fertile Crescent since the Neolithic and celebrated in Levantine kitchens for golden شوربة عدس ('lentil soup').

history.meaning: lentils (also the origin of عَدَسَة 'optical lens', shaped like a lentil)

عدسة.etymology: Singulative noun عَدَسَة ('a single lentil; optical lens') from collective عَدَس ('lentils'). Medieval Arab opticians—most famously Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) in Kitāb al-Manāẓir—named convex glass lenses عدسة because their biconvex curvature resembles a lentil seed; Latin translators calqued this directly as lens ('lentil'), giving English 'lens'!

cognates.meaning: from Latin lens ('lentil'), matching Arabic عدسة

عسل.etymology: Native Arabic noun from the root ع-س-ل ('-s-l), naming bee honey and prized since pre-Islamic poetry for sweetness and healing.
عسل.notes: Served across Jordan at breakfast alongside warm bread, olive oil, or tea.

عمة.etymology: Feminine of عَمّ (ʿamm, 'paternal uncle'), from ancient Semitic kinship root ع-م-م (ʿ-m-m, 'father's kin, paternal clan').

عين.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *'ayn- ('eye; natural water spring'), grammatically feminine.
عين.notes: Gives rise to warm Levantine expressions of affection and delight such as يا عيني ('oh my!', literally 'oh my eye') and على عيني ('gladly').

غابة.etymology: Noun غَابَة ('forest, dense woodland', plural غَابَات) from the hollow root غ-ي-ب ('be hidden, disappear from sight'), originally naming a thicket of trees or reeds dense enough to conceal whoever enters it.

غرفة.etymology: From the triliteral root غ-ر-ف (gh-r-f), originally 'to scoop up water by hand', which developed an architectural sense of a raised upper chamber or room.
غرفة.notes: Classical Arabic distinguished an upper room (غُرفة) before the word generalized to any room.

غسل.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *rḫṣ / Arabic root غ-س-ل (gh-s-l, 'to wash with water'), one of the core everyday domestic verbs across all varieties of Arabic.

فانوس.etymology: Borrowed via Byzantine/Medieval Greek φανός (phanós, 'torch, lantern', from φαίνω 'to shine, appear').
فانوس.notes: Takes the broken plural فوانيس, familiar across Amman courtyards and verandas.

فجر.etymology: Classical Arabic فَجْر ('dawn, daybreak') from the root ف-ج-ر ('cleave open, burst forth'), vividly picturing the first streak of morning light splitting open the darkness of night along the eastern horizon.

فخار.etymology: Classical Arabic فُخَّار / فَخَّار (faḫḫār, 'fired pottery, stoneware'), inherited from Aramaic פַּחָרָא (paḥḥārā, 'potter, earthenware'), ultimately from Akkadian paḫāru ('potter').

فرشاية.etymology: Levantine singulative noun فُرْشَايَة ('paintbrush, brush', plural فرشايات), adapted from post-classical فُرْشَاة / فُرْشَة and tied in popular usage to the root ف-ر-ش ('spread evenly across a surface').

فرن.etymology: Early Mediterranean cultural borrowing into Arabic (فُرْن furn) via Aramaic פּוּרְנָא (pūrnā) from Latin furnus ('baking oven, vaulted kiln').
فرن.notes: In Amman and across the Levant, فرن names both a home kitchen oven and the neighbourhood bread bakery.

فطور.etymology: From the root ف-ط-ر (f-t-r, 'to split, break open, break a fast'), naming the morning meal that breaks the night's fast—exact parallel to English 'breakfast'.
فطور.notes: The related Form IV verbal noun إفطار refers especially to breaking the Ramadan fast at sunset, while فطور is everyday morning breakfast in Amman.

فنجان.etymology: Borrowed from Persian *pingān / finjān* ('cup, small bowl', originally a water-clock bowl measuring time).
فنجان.notes: In Jordan فنجان (plural فناجين) specifically names a handleless Arabic coffee cup or porcelain teacup, distinct from كاسة ('drinking glass').

فندق.etymology: Borrowed via Aramaic from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon, 'inn welcoming all travellers', from πᾶς 'all' + δέχομαι 'to receive').
فندق.notes: Entered Arabic in the early medieval period for a merchant caravanserai or travellers' inn, and today means 'hotel'.

فولاذ.etymology: Classical Arabic borrowing فُولَاذ ('crucible steel, tempered steel') from Middle Persian pōlāwad (modern Persian پولاد pūlād), celebrated historically for Damascus and Khorasan blades and today used for high-tensile steel wire.

قائمة.etymology: Feminine active participle (فَاعِلَة) of قَامَ (qāma, 'to stand upright'), from root ق-و-م: a vertical column or standing register of items, hence a written 'list' or café 'menu'.

قرفة.etymology: From the Arabic root ق-ر-ف (q-r-f, 'to peel off bark or rind'), naming cinnamon directly as fragrant peeled tree bark.
قرفة.notes: Warm cinnamon rolls and spiced tea are winter favourites in Amman.

قصد.etymology: From the root ق-ص-د (q-s-d), whose core sense is heading straight toward an aim or target, and by extension intending or meaning something.
قصد.notes: In Jordanian speech قصد with possessive suffixes (قصدي 'I mean', قصدك 'you mean') clarifies a speaker's point.

قطار.etymology: Classical Arabic قِطَار originally named a 'single-file caravan of camels linked head-to-tail' (from the root ق-ط-ر 'line up in file, drip in sequence'); in the 19th century, coupled railway carriages were naturally given the same vivid name: 'train'.

history.meaning: file of camels strung one behind another

قلب.etymology: From the Semitic root ق-ل-ب (q-l-b, 'to turn, invert, change'), naming the heart as the ever-turning centre of feeling and thought.

قلم.etymology: Early borrowing (via Aramaic or Ethiopic) from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos, 'reed, reed pen').
قلم.notes: Combines in compounds such as قلم رصاص ('pencil', literally 'lead pen') and قلم حبر ('ink pen').

قميص.etymology: Classical Arabic قَمِيص ('shirt, tunic', plural قُمْصَان), borrowed in Late Antiquity from Late Latin camisia ('linen shirt, nightshirt') via Greek καμίσιον, and later re-exported from Andalusi Arabic into Iberian Romance.

قهوة.etymology: Classical Arabic قَهْوة originally denoted a dark, appetite-suppressing beverage (historically wine) before shifting in Yemen during the 15th century to the roasted coffee brew.
قهوة.notes: From Arabic قهوة passed into Ottoman Turkish kahve, Italian caffè, and English 'coffee'.

كاحل.etymology: Classical anatomical noun كَاحِل ('ankle', plural كَوَاحِل) on the pattern فَاعِل from the root ك-ح-ل, designating the joint between the foot and the lower leg.

كتاب.etymology: From the Semitic triliteral root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b, 'to write'), formed on the verbal-noun/object pattern فِعال (fiʿāl) denoting 'that which is written together' — hence a letter, document, or book.

كرسي.etymology: An ancient Near Eastern culture word traceable through Aramaic *kursyā* and Akkadian *kussû* ultimately to Sumerian *gu-za* ('chair, throne').
كرسي.notes: Takes the broken plural كراسي in both Standard and Jordanian Arabic.

كعب.etymology: Classical Arabic noun كَعْب ('heel, anklebone; cube', plural كِعَاب / كُعُوب) from the Semitic root ك-ع-ب ('protrude squarely, form a knuckle/joint'). Its square die-bone shape also gave rise to مُكَعَّب ('cube') and الكَعْبَة ('the Cube / Kaaba').

history.meaning: heel of the foot or shoe

كهربا.etymology: Levantine colloquial form of كَهْرَباء (kahrabāʾ, 'electricity'), borrowed from Persian کهربا (kahrubā, literally 'straw-attractor', i.e. amber, from kāh 'straw' + rubā 'attracting'), mirroring Greek ἤλεκτρον ('amber' -> 'electricity').

لحن.etymology: Classical Arabic لَحْن (laḥn, 'melody, musical mode, cadence of voice'), from root ل-ح-ن denoting modulated intonation and song.

لوز.etymology: Ancient Semitic collective noun لَوْز ('almonds'), native to the rocky hillsides of Jordan and the Levant. Borrowed via Andalusi Arabic اللَّوْزَة into Portuguese tramela/alloza.

ليمون.etymology: Entered Arabic from Persian *līmūn* (ultimately of Indo-Aryan/Austronesian citrus origin), and travelled from Arabic into medieval Mediterranean Europe as English 'lemon'.
ليمون.notes: Collective noun in Jordanian Arabic; a single whole lemon is counted as حبة ليمون.

متر.etymology: International metric unit مِتْر ('metre', plural أَمْتَار), borrowed in the 19th century from French mètre, itself from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure, rule')—fully naturalized into Arabic broken-plural morphology (متر -> أمتار).

مخدة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِخَدَّة ('pillow, cushion', plural مَخَدَّات) built with prefix مِـ on خَدّ ('cheek', geminate root خ-د-د): literally 'a cheek-rest' on which a sleeper lays their cheek.

مخطط.etymology: Passive participle مُخَطَّط ('floor plan, blueprint, layout; striped') from Form II خَطَّطَ ('draw lines, map out'), built on the geminate root خ-ط-ط ('carve or draw a line, خط').

مربى.etymology: Passive participle of Form II رَبَّى (rabbā, 'to nurture, cure, preserve in syrup'), from root ر-ب-و: fruit preserved slowly in sugar.

history.meaning: fruit preserve; confection cured in honey or sugar

مرتبان.etymology: Beloved Levantine pantry word مَرْتَبَان (also spelled مَرْطَبَان, 'glass or glazed storage jar'), named after the historic Burmese port city of Martaban (Mottama), whose glazed stoneware jars carried spices, preserves, sugar, and pickles across Indian Ocean and Ottoman trade routes into Syrian and Jordanian kitchens.

history.meaning: glazed spice and preserve jar from Martaban

مروحة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِرْوَحَة ('fan, ventilator') formed on the pattern مِفْعَلَة from the hollow root ر-و-ح ('blow gently, breeze, refresh'), originally naming a woven palm-leaf hand fan and in modern Arabic any electric cooling fan.

مسطرة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْطَرَة ('ruler, straightedge', plural مَسَاطِر) formed with prefix مِـ from the root س-ط-ر ('rule straight lines, write in neat rows').

مسمار.etymology: Instrumental noun مِسْمَار ('nail, metal pin, peg', plural مَسَامِير) formed on the pattern مِفْعَال from the Semitic root س-م-ر ('fasten tightly with nails').

مصروف.etymology: Passive participle of ص-ر-ف (s-r-f) on the pattern مفعول, literally 'that which is spent or disbursed', used as a noun for everyday expenses or pocket money.
مصروف.notes: The root ص-ر-ف covers turning, exchanging currency, and spending money.

مطبخ.etymology: Noun of place on the pattern مَفْعَل (maf'al) from the Semitic root ط-ب-خ (t-b-kh, 'to cook'), literally 'place of cooking'.
مطبخ.notes: Regular place-noun formation alongside مدخل ('entrance') and مكتب ('office/desk').

مطر.etymology: Inherited Semitic weather noun from م-ط-ر (m-t-r, 'to rain'), cognate with Hebrew *māṭār* and Ugaritic *mṭr*.
مطر.notes: Winter rain (مطر الشتا) feeds Amman's gardens and stone cisterns.

مطرقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِطْرَقَة ('hammer') formed with the tool prefix مِـ (mi-) on the root ط-ر-ق ('to strike, knock, forge metal'). In a piano, the same word names each felt-covered wooden hammer striking the strings.

معطف.etymology: Instrumental garment noun مِعْطَف ('coat, overcoat', plural مَعَاطِف) formed with prefix مِـ from the root ع-ط-ف ('bend around, fold over affectionately'), literally 'a garment wrapped warmly around the shoulders'.

مفتاح.etymology: Instrumental noun on the pattern مِفْعال (mif'āl) from the root ف-ت-ح (f-t-h, 'to open'), literally 'an instrument for opening'.
مفتاح.notes: In Jordanian Arabic مفتاح covers both a door key and a mechanic's spanner or wrench.

مقام.etymology: Noun of place/standing مَقَام ('standing place, station, musical mode/key') built with prefix مَـ on the hollow root ق-و-م ('stand, rise'). In Arab musical theory since the medieval treatises, مقام names the tonal scale/mode (and by extension a piece's key) on which a melody rests.

مقعد.etymology: Noun of place (مَفْعَد) from root ق-ع-د (q-ʿ-d, 'to sit down'): literally 'a place for sitting', hence a chair seat or garden bench.

مقهى.etymology: Noun of place مَقْهًى ('coffeehouse, café', plural مَقَاهٍ / مقاهي) formed with the locative prefix مَـ from قَهْوَة ('coffee'), literally 'the place where coffee is brewed and shared'.

ملح.etymology: Inherited Proto-Semitic primary noun مِلْح ('salt') from `*milḥ-`, conserved unchanged for millennia across Arabic, Hebrew, and Aramaic—and central to the Arab ethic of hospitality (عيش وملح, 'bread and salt').

ملعقة.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْعَقَة ('spoon') formed with prefix مِـ on the root ل-ع-ق ('lick, sip honey or soup'). In spoken Jordanian and Palestinian Arabic, harmless metathesis shifts مِلْعَقَة to مَعْلَقَة (ma'laqa).

ملقط.etymology: Instrumental noun مِلْقَط ('tweezers, tongs') formed with the tool pattern مِفْعَل on the root ل-ق-ط ('pick up, glean tiny things from the ground').

ممر.etymology: Noun of place (ism makān) on the pattern مَفْعَل (mafʿal) from the geminate root م-ر-ر (m-r-r, 'to pass, go through'), literally 'a place of passing' — a corridor, hallway, or walkway.

منشفة.etymology: Instrumental noun on the feminine pattern مِفْعَلَة (mif'ala) from ن-ش-ف (n-sh-f, 'to dry, absorb moisture'), literally 'a drying cloth, towel'.
منشفة.notes: Plural مناشف; directly transparent alongside the adjective ناشف ('dry').

ميزانية.etymology: Abstract noun in -iyya built on مِيزَان (mīzān, 'pair of scales, balance'), itself an instrument noun (مِفْعَال) from root و-ز-ن (w-z-n, 'to weigh'): weighing income against expenditure ('budget').

نحاس.etymology: Inherited Semitic metal term (*nuḥāš-, 'copper, brass, bronze'), naming the warm yellow-red metal prized by Levantine smiths for keys, trays, and valves.

نظارة.etymology: Intensive instrumental feminine noun نَظَّارَة ('eyeglasses, spectacles') coined on the pattern فَعَّالَة from the Semitic root ن-ظ-ر ('look, observe, gaze attentively').

نعنع.etymology: Reduplicated aromatic plant noun (نَعْنَع / نَعْنَاع naʿnaʿ) of ancient Semitic heritage, attested across Arabic and Aramaic for garden mint.

نور.etymology: From the hollow root ن-و-ر (n-w-r, 'light, illumination, blossom'), related to نار ('fire') and منارة ('lighthouse, minaret').
نور.notes: Appears both as a beloved Arabic given name (نور) and in the classic morning reply صباح النور ('morning of light').

وتر.etymology: Ancient Semitic noun وَتَر ('bowstring; musical string', plural أَوْتَار) from the root و-ت-ر ('draw taut'). From early lutes and qanuns to modern pianos, أوتار names the stretched strings whose vibration produces musical pitch.

ياسمين.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Persian *yāsamīn* ('jasmine flower'), fragrant climbing shrub cultivated across Levantine courtyards for centuries.
ياسمين.notes: From Arabic and Persian the word entered medieval Latin and French *jasmin*, giving English 'jasmine'.

يد.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *yad- ('hand, arm, handle'), grammatically feminine because body parts in pairs are feminine in Arabic.
يد.notes: In spoken Jordanian, 'hand' is pronounced إيد (īd, plural إيدين), while يد (yadd) also names a door handle or tool grip.

يعني.etymology: Originally the third-person masculine singular imperfect of عنى ('to mean, intend', root ع-ن-ي), literally 'it means'. In spoken Levantine Arabic it grammaticalized into a versatile discourse marker ('so, that is, I mean').
يعني.notes: Learners hear يعني both as a literal verb ('that means') and as a natural conversational bridge.
